image_description:
## 1) Chart type
Faceted vertical bar chart (small-multiple time-series bar charts), with one panel per city.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples** by **city**
- **Unequal panel sizes**: some cities (notably New Delhi) are shown in larger panels
- **Color encoding** applied to bars to indicate pollution level / air quality category
- **No stacking** visible

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Date / day (Nov ’18 to Nov ’19) | Temporal | Position on x-axis within each panel |
| PM2.5 concentration (µg/m³) | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Air quality level / EPA AQI category (Good, Unhealthy, Hazardous, Extreme) | Ordinal | Color/hue of bars |
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel labels |
| PM2.5 concentration scale reference | Quantitative | Legend scale and y-axis annotations/gridlines |

Notes visible in the chart:
- Title indicates the subject is **daily average air pollution around the world**
- The legend explicitly links color to **PM2.5 concentration** and **E.P.A. Air Quality Index** categories.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the cities with the most air pollution were Delhi, India, Beijing, Chine, and Kampala, Uganda. I also saw how Nairobi, Kenya as well as Manhattan, USA having fairly nice air quality. Along with that, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia and San Francisco, U.S.A have pretty good air quality, except for each of them having one large spike, Kuala Lumpur later in the day, and San Francisco very early in the day. Mexico city is on the worse, side, although at most times it is medium with few spikes of dangerous. Finally, I saw that Los Angeles, USA, Paris, France and Sao Paulo, Brazil have fairly good air quality, although at most times it is average.
2. I wonder why cities like Delhi, India, Kampala, Uganda, as well as Beijing, China have such horrible air quality. I also wonder how Nairobi, Kenya, Manhattan, U.S., and Tokyo, Japan have such good air quality. I also wonder what the red spikes in the graphs of Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and San Francisco are.
3. A lack of air quality is very dangerous to human beings, as it can cause many diseases and simply make it more difficult to breathe. I was born in and am from India, and can relate because I lived in Mumbai, India, a city which is also known for bad air quality. Having experienced this I know how it feels to be in that type of an environment, and the smells that come with it, as well as how harmful it can be.
4. Air Quality: It Could be Life or Death for you

By observing the places with high pollution emissions, we can find the root cause of this disruption and try instead using technology that is used in cleaner places such as Manhattan.

comments.raw_comment:
< Air Pollution:  Lapses and Rehabilitation >
I am immediately aware that this graph shows the passage of time between November of 2018 and November of 2019. This seems strange, considering that this time-frame is when the world did not have more pressing matters to concern itself with. However, it does seem to provide insight into a time that some of us may consider irrelevant. I wonder which policies allowed certain cities, such as San Francisco and Beijing, to better their air quality, while some others have either stagnated or are worse off than before. Seeing as how I am currently living outside of these cities, this won't have much direct impact on my community or myself. However, it does show that we can reduce pollution with the right initiative. So, I hope that the community that I am residing in can follow suit. I do think that it would have been interesting to compare this graph to its modern counterpart. Also, while it would take substantially more work to put together, a global take on this data could provide some interesting insight. If this were to occur, then a more simplified graph may be needed to represent the information properly.

I noticed that the cities with the most air pollution include Kampala, Beijing, and New Delhi, with New Delhi being the most intense. In cities such as Mexico City and Kuala Lumpur, the average air pollution is in the orange spectrum, but their graphs contain some red spikes. This is similar to San Francisco with on average good air quality but also has some red spikes. I wonder what causes these red spikes. For places such as Beijing and New Delhi, I wonder if the air pollution has more to do with factories and production sites rather than population and fuel usage. I find it rather surprising that Manhattan's graph is similar to Nairobi's, Tokyo's, LA's, Paris's, and Sao Paulo's - all with relatively good air quality. I wonder if misinformation or urban stereotypes causes me and other to think that Manhattan would have worse air quality. Since these graphs show the average air pollution in 2018 and 2019, I wonder what these graphs look like now. 

This impacts the community because it's useful when proposing pollution regulations. I live in a place with relatively clean air, and I think this information is still relevant to me. It's even more helpful to those who live in those specific cities as they can use this information to address their air pollution issues. Air pollution is a serious matter as it affects both the quality of life and the quality of the environment. 

A headline could be "Sharing the Same Air but Breathing Differently: Global Average Air Pollution".

Noticings:
I notice right off the bat that New Delhi has the most extreme and worst air pollution, reaching up to 500ug/m^3 and that Kenya had the healthiest air quality out of the cities listed. I also notice that very often there are cities that experience small periods of very bad air quality, but then go back down, what causes this change in air? 

Wonderings:
I wonder what caused San Francisco to have a spike in air pollution because for the most part, they are in the green section for having good air quality. Does population contribute to a city's air quality? I wonder why Los Angeles and Manhattan were not as bad as some of the other cities?

Impacts:
These graphs let us know where it might be safer to travel to in regards to air pollution and quality. It also gives us a clear look into what major cities need to do more in order to improve their air quality. The air quality in these major cities affect everything around including people's health and their communities. It's important we pay attention and act based on the city's needs.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that Manhattan, Tokyo, Nairobi, Los Angeles, Paris, and Brazil have consistently low rates not usually reaching unhealthy levels and usually below 25 micrograms per cubic meter. I notice that Kampala has fairly consistent rates that could be unhealthy with brief exceptions. I notice that Kuala Lumpur and San Fransisco have low rates of particulate pollution (San Fransisco usually below 25 micrograms per cubic meter, and Kuala Lumpur remaining below 50 micrograms per cubic meter) except for a brief spike when it was approximately 150 micrograms per cubic meter. Kampala is usually from 50 micrograms per cubic meter to 75 micrograms per cubic meter with a few outliers. New Delhi has exceptionally high levels starting at about 350 micrograms per cubic centimeter and forming a negative slope until the outliers at the end. Bejing starts with an average of 175 micrograms per cubic meter then dropping to about 25 micrograms per cubic meter before rising to 100 micrograms per cubic meter at the end. 
I wonder what causes the spikes in micrograms per cubic meter. Could it possibly be caused by fires, destruction of buildings resulting in particulate pollution? I wonder why the population of the countries isn't proportionate in many cases for especially in the case, of San Paolo, Tokyo, and Mexico City. 
A possible title could be "Air Pollution: Invisible Until It's Too Late".

Thanks to all students who responded. We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these graphs:  “Is Your Air Just Air?” by Conner of Iowa, “Air Pollution Poisoning Many Cities From Around the World." By Ashley of Massachusetts, “Global Air Pollution Trends: Some Cities Breath Easy, While Others Long for a Breath of Fresh Air” by Jacki of Switzerland, “Death in the Air.  O, So Much Despair!” by Mia of Washington, “Air Pollution, the Silent Killer” by Tegan of Kimball Union Academy in Meriden, New Hampshire, and “What Air Do You Breathe In?” by Kayleigh McDonald, Pennsylvania.
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Feb. 26 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.

comments.raw_comment: Based on the data displayed on the graph, our group noticed several important observations. The first being that of the various cities, New Delhi had the highest amount of air pollution. Much of the pollution in New Delhi occurs during the winter months. The air in New Dehli often remains in the unhealthy to hazardous range. San Francisco had a large spike in November of 2018, but it has been steady since then. Kuala Lumpur also had a large spike in the middle of seemingly steady pollution rates. Based on these observations, we wonder what causes the air pollution in Beijing and New Delhi to fluctuate so much. We also wondered What caused the large spikes in Kuala Lumpur and San Francisco and how did San Francisco improve its air quality after the spike? Lastly, we analyzed what impact these findings had on ourselves and our community. Air pollution plays a major role in not only our health but also the health of the surrounding community. Furthermore, significant pollution can have harmful effects on the economy, health care system, and decreases quality of life. If the pollution is too bad and causes harmful side effects, population numbers can decrease as people stop moving to the area or move out. Based on the data, we would title this article, “Now and then, here and air: Major Cities get Polluted :(“

We also happen to wonder why throughout the more time that passes why it happens to spike so much. Another thing we noticed is the spike in pollution in the the middle of some random year in cities like Mexico City, Kuala Lumpur, and even San Francisco. We wonder what causes these cities in particular to spike during these months, was there a festival of sorts? We also wondered how a city such as Manhattan is so low in pollution compared to even Paris, a place where you would think there were to be way less pollution.

Group 5: Macy, Grace, Lynzie, Musa
We noticed that the air is the most unhealthy in the city of New Delhi, as it is almost at the hazardous level. Nairobi, Kenya and Manhattan are the cities shown with the healthiest air. Cities like Beijing and Kampala, Uganda also have pretty unhealthy air. We wonder why the air is so bad in these huge cities with so many people living in them. We also wonder if there is anything being done at the moment to help the cities with air pollution that is hazardous. Finally, we wonder what is causing the unhealthy air in some of these cities and how the air got so bad. The impact this has on our community is that it could be dangerous for the people in these cities. Having unhealthy air could cause health issues for some people, especially if they live in one of the cities with a high amount of unhealthy air.

“Air Pollution: Is Your City at Risk?”

Our group noticed many things in this graph, such as Nairobi and Manhattan have the best air quality out of all the cities. The size and population of the city does not determine the air quality as Los Angeles is a huge city, but has good air quality. New Delhi has the worst air quality out of all the cities. New Delhi is the only city that reaches the extreme in the air quality index. There is a key to represent the different colors on the graph. Green and yellow mean good air quality, while red and orange mean unhealthy or hazardous air quality. Our group wondered what happened in San Francisco to cause such a big spike in air pollution and why famous tourist cities like Paris or Manhattan have low pollution levels. We wondered what the X-axis represents and why a lot of cities show spikes in air quality levels. We also wondered why New Delhi has the worst air quality, is it because they have a lot of factories that pollute gases? This impacts us and our community because if the air is too polluted, it can cause a lot of health issues, and overall it is bad for the environment.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the daily average air pollution in a dozen major cities from around the world for the year Nov. 2018 – Oct. 2019.  Note that all graphs use the same scale to show the number of micrograms per cubic meter of outdoor particulate pollution.  .

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next graphs on smoking will be released by Friday, Feb. 26, 2021 with moderation on Wednesday, March 3.

I notice that most of the cities stay similar. Some of the cities have spikes in air pollution like San Francisco, while in Nairobi the air pollution stays pretty steady. I also notice that New Delhi has a very high amount of air pollution. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what happened in San Francisco to cause such a high spike in air pollution. I was thinking maybe a fire because it is in California. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live in the suburbs so the air pollution isn't as high. I don’t think Boston's air pollution is nearly as high as some of the other major cities, but there's definitely air pollution.

What I notice:
- Uganda and New Delhi are the cities with the most red
- [Kuala Lumper, Malaysia], San Francisco, and Beijing are the cities that spiked into red then are back down 
- Most of the cities that are red have big cities or lots of cars (smoke as well) 
- New Delhi is in the lead, the only city going to the extreme range as well as succeeding to stay in red the longest
- Most of the cities have a stable color or range and then it spikes up and then back down again
- New Delhi, Kuala Lumpur, and Beijing are all capital cities 
Questions I have:
* are the cities that have higher air pollution also the ones that have more air pollution deaths?
* are the cities that have lower air pollution farther from factories or have lots of trees?
* why did all cities spike up and and then come down?
* are the cities that have higher air pollution also have higher population of people?
* when some cities reached the extreme range, did everyone stay inside because then it dropped right back down?
* why do some cities in the same continent have very different air rates?
* are the cities that have higher air pollution bigger cities than the others?

A catchy headline could be: Rates of a Deadly Thing, Pollution

comments.raw_comment: I notice that this is a graph displaying the different air qualities throughout November 2018 to November 2019 in a select few of the major cities around the world. I can see that a few cities like Nairobi and Manhattan are in the healthier side, Los Angeles and Paris are in the unhealthy side while Kampala and Beijing are in very extreme air quality areas. I wonder as to why it is that we see these cities struggling with air quality. I can see that Malaysia and Beijing are both in Asia so it makes me wonder if the density of a region has any influence to its air quality, given that Asia is an extremely dense continent. I also wonder as to why is it that Manhattan is fairly well with air quality while Los Angeles is struggling -- why is it that the coasts vary from air pollution? The impact that this has on my community is not a great deal, but it is definitely a good idea to keep an eye on  air quality as a healthy life style. Given that Manhattan and Boston are relatively close areas, I can assume that the air quality is similar and more on the healthy side. Whenever I check the weather for Boston I always see the air quality index towards the green side, which is always a good sign. Potential catchy headline: "What is Air Quality Like in Major World Cities?"

•	What do you notice?
Many of the places only have a few times when they are in the green, most of the time they are in the yellow or orange looking color. I also notice that there are times when there is no pollution or no record. I used to live in Beijing for 5 years and I thought it was bad I would be afraid to live in New Delhi.


•	What do you wonder?
I wonder why those few times with no record what is going on. Is it no record or a period of no pollution? If it is a period of no pollution what is going on that there is no pollution. It is the same for the green times. What are they doing that they have no pollution? 

•	What impact does this have on you and your community?
Pollution like Beijing has a big impact on the community. There were times we were not allowed to go outside because the pollution was too high. Sometimes this would last for weeks. We had to wear masks all the time due to the pollution. Sometimes they would close the schools because it got too high. Not only the schools but no cars could be driven, and factories had to be shut down. That put people out of work and no school for days.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that most of the cities with unhealthy and hazardous air pollution are outside of the United States. For example, New Delhi, Beijing, and Kampala, Uganda have the worst average air pollution than any other country and the three United States cities in the graph. I notice that the air pollution in New Delhi is more than three times the levels than the city with the second highest level of air pollution, Beijing. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the air quality in New Delhi is so bad. What factors have caused the air pollution to get so high?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live very close to Manhattan. I had always assumed that the pollution levels in Manhattan are extremely high. However, when put into perspective with other major cities around the globe, the air pollution in Manhattan does not seem as bad as I once thought. However, the people in my community should still do the most they can to avoid creating unnecessary air pollution when possible. For example, we should try carpooling when possible.
